source_text: Iuraverit falso. Iusiurandum mendax nomen Dei usurpat. Sit timor iuramenti.
orientation: Origen is listing sins that require confession and restitution, now turning to the sin of swearing falsely.
pass_a_gloss: He will have sworn falsely. An oath lying [the] name [of] God usurps. Let there be fear [of] oath-taking.

choices.why: Perfect subjunctive in a conditional or generalizing context; rendered as a plain perfect to keep the force of a completed act.
Adjective mendax modifies the noun oath; kept as adjective-noun to preserve the compact Latin phrase.
The verb means to seize or take for oneself unlawfully; 'usurps' captures the wrongful appropriation of God's name.

choices.english: Let there be fear of an oath
choices.why: Jussive subjunctive expressing a command or exhortation; kept as 'let there be' to preserve the imperative force.
rejected: There should be fear of an oath

pass_b_english: He has sworn falsely. A lying oath usurps the name of God. Let there be fear of an oath.

last_rejected.quote: Let there be fear of an oath
last_rejected.why: Imperative 'sit' is jussive/exhortative 'let there be', but context demands 'may there be' or 'there should be' as moral prescription, not command to reader.
last_rejected.fix: There must be fear of swearing an oath.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Sit' as jussive subjunctive naturally renders 'let there be'; 'may there be' is a preference, not a meaning change.
